top_cited_works.title: Development and Optical Emission Spectroscopy Characterization of a 13.56 MHz RF Plasma Source
top_cited_works.abstract: This paper presents the development of a radio-frequency (RF) plasma source capable of operating on molecular gases and its initial physical testing and characterization via optical emission spectroscopy (OES). The plasma source has a cylindrical geometry and is powered by a 13.56 MHz radio frequency (RF) power supply. The source is designed to serve as a testbed for molecular plasma investigations in support of electric propulsion applications. The source’s thermal limits, pressure capabilities, and coupling efficiency were first evaluated. Then, broadband (time-averaged) survey spectra were obtained for species identification and to study specific non-equilibrium plasma temperatures. A rovibrational fit was performed using the Specair non-equilibrium code for spectra collected during operation on nitrogen and specific rotational and vibrational temperatures are reported.

top_cited_works.title: Influence of Laser Energy and Ignition Location on Spray Flame Evolution
top_cited_works.abstract: Laser ignition experiments were performed in a heptane spray using an Nd:YAG laser to investigate its ignitability. In the first set, Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) and imaging were employed to quantify Hα/O ratios, kernel size, and kernel number at various locations within the spray. While these parameters generally followed the spray profile, they did not reliably predict ignition. In the second set, OH chemiluminescence, LIBS, and high-speed imaging was utilized to understand the effect of laser energy and ignition location on ignitability. Two distinct modes of ignition failure – short and long – were identified based on kernel extinction time. For the spray conditions studied, ignition was achieved at laser energy of 250 mJ, while long-mode failure occurred at 80 mJ, and short-mode failure at 30 mJ. Optical intensities of OH and CH showed that higher laser energies generated more radical species and sustained the flame long enough to establish stable ignition. Additionally, kernel trajectories extracted from high-speed images showed that ignition is more probable for cases where the spark is generated in or moves into recirculation zone. recent_works.title: LIF Diagnostics of Molecular Propellants: A Study of N 2 + in a Hidden Anode Plasma Source
recent_works.abstract: Molecular propellants are increasingly relevant for future electric propulsion systems, yet quantitative plasma diagnostics for these species remain underdeveloped. This contribution presents further advances in laser–induced fluorescence (LIF) on N2+ in a plasma–thruster–relevant device, using a Hidden Anode Plasma Contactor as a testbed. An improved excitation scheme based on the ��2Σ+�� → ��2Σ+�� (0, 0) ��(9) transition is implemented to reduce intrinsicspin–rotation splitting and minimize the need for spectral deconvolution. Spatially resolved Ion Velocity Distribution Functions (IVDFs) measurements up to 40 mm downstream reveal that significant ion acceleration begins only beyond 10–15 mm. Strong, low velocity tails indicate delayed ionization in the expanding molecular plume. The inferred potential drops are compared with emissive probe measurements of the plasma potential and with far plume ion energy distributions from a Retarding Potential Analyzer (RPA) probe, showing close agreement. These results validate the diagnostic in a molecular plasma and establish N2+ LIF as a robust tool for velocity–resolved characterization of nitrogen–based thruster concepts.

recent_works.title: Towards Plasma Assisted Stabilization of a Natural Gas Burner Using Nanosecond Pulsed Discharges
recent_works.abstract: This study investigates the stability limits of a benchtop combustor and the potential use of plasma-assisted combustion (PAC) to improve flame stability and emissions characteristics. Baseline flame stability (without plasma) using natural gas was studied in the open-flame configuration across a wide range of equivalence ratios (ϕ = 0.27–0.87) and thermal input powers (25–100 kBTU/hr). Flame dynamics were assessed using imagery, acoustic, and emission measurements. Results showed that in lean conditions blowout was never observed. Instead, lean flames tend to transition to a low-intensity pilot flame that remains present over the entire lean operating regime. This behavior reflects the burner’s staged design, whereby fuel is injected into a rich primary zone and entrains air through a series of ports upstream of the igniter. For a fixed equivalence ratio, increasing the burner power resulted in a noticeable decrease in flame intensity and sound power. This was accompanied by an increase in CO emissions, suggesting a reduction in combustion efficiency.
